title: The ship that lied
pull: A fake flag, a real prize

facts.text: On 6 November 1941, a month and a day before Pearl Harbor, the cruiser USS Omaha and the destroyer USS Somers were on Neutrality Patrol in the Atlantic when they sighted a freighter at dawn near the equator, between Brazil and Africa.
The freighter flew the American flag and had "Willmoto, Philadelphia" painted on her hull and stern. A U.S. flag was painted on a hatch cover too.
She was really the German motorship Odenwald of the Hamburg America Line. She had left Yokohama, Japan, on 21 August 1941, trying to slip past the British blockade.
Her holds carried about 3,857 metric tons of raw rubber from Asia, plus truck tires and other cargo, roughly 6,200 tons in all. Germany needed rubber badly.
She steered to dodge the Americans and gave poor answers to their signals. Omaha's captain, Theodore E. Chandler, ordered her to stop and sent over an armed boarding party.
As the sailors came aboard, two explosions went off in the stern. The Germans had set scuttling charges, signaled that the ship was sinking, and taken to the lifeboats.
The Americans ordered the crew back aboard, plugged the flooding and got the engines running again. By that evening the ship was under way at about 9.5 knots.
The United States was not at war, so the legal ground was shaky. A National Archives photo caption says Chandler, unsure of his legal ground, boarded her on "suspicion of slave trading."
With an American prize crew aboard, escorted by Omaha and Somers, Odenwald reached San Juan, Puerto Rico, on 17 November 1941. The United States sued for salvage the next day.
On 24 December 1941 the government took title to the rubber cargo for the American war effort.

On 30 April 1947 the federal court in Puerto Rico ruled for the sailors, and an appeals court upheld it in 1948. Each man in the boarding party received $3,000, and every other man on Omaha and Somers got two months' pay and allowances.
The award is often called the last prize money the U.S. Navy ever paid, though the court actually granted it as salvage for saving an abandoned ship.

After Germany declared war on the United States on 11 December 1941, the ship was taken into American service and renamed Blenheim. She carried cargo for the United States, went to the Army in 1945, and was sold for scrap in 1948.

declassified.fact: Captain Theodore Chandler, who ordered the boarding, rose to rear admiral. In January 1945, in the Philippines, a kamikaze struck the flag bridge of his flagship, USS Louisville. Badly burned, he hauled fire hoses alongside his enlisted sailors, then waited his turn for first aid with them. He died the next day.
